t: for the verse converted it into a positive commandment, that if he robbed he must return. The negative commandment ("you shall not rob") was converted into a positive commandment ("and he shall return the robbed item"), and one does not receive lashes for such a negative commandment (Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:2).

and even if he burned the robbed item he does not receive lashes, etc.. Although for a negative commandment converted into a positive one, if he did not fulfill the positive commandment he receives lashes, and he should have received lashes since he did not return the robbed item, he is nonetheless exempt from lashes for another reason: since he must pay the value of the robbed item, and no negative commandment that carries a payment obligation incurs lashes (there, and see also Hilchot Genevah 1:1).
and it is forbidden to rob anything by Torah law. By the Torah it is forbidden to rob even less than the value of a perutah (except that there is no obligation to return it, as below 5:6).
even a gentile who serves idolatry it is forbidden to rob. See also Hilchot Genevah 1:1.
for example, that he snatched movable property from his hand. And with robbing land too he transgresses a negative commandment (Hilchot Genevah 7:11).
or that he overpowered his slaves and his animals. Seized them by force.
and used them. See below 3:6-7.
or that he went down into his field and ate its fruit. See below 9:5.
with the owners' consent. Unlike robbery, where the item came into his hand without the owners' consent.
for example, he had a loan or a deposit in his fellow's hand. That he lent to his fellow or deposited with him.

or wages. It seems this means that his fellow worked for him as a hired worker and he holds his wages in his hand and does not give them to him. And although in this case the fellow did not give him money, it is still included in the prohibition of oppression (see Sefer HaMitzvot, Negative Commandment 238, Hilchot Sechirut 11:2).
violent and hard. A violent person with whom it is hard to litigate.

the Sages enacted for the sake of the repentant that he give its value and not lose the building. They made an enactment to ease matters for robbers who wish to repent, since if returning the robbed item itself would cause a loss, it would make it hard for robbers to return to the right path (and see below halachah 13 and below 2:2 for further enactments to ease matters for the repentant).
and made it into the roof of a sukkah for the festival. He built it into the sukkah of the festival of Sukkot (see also Hilchot Sukkah 5:25).

he gives him its value. Since he fulfills a commandment with it, it is treated as a permanent building into which the enactment for the repentant applies on the festival, even though in itself it is not a permanent structure (Rashi and Meiri, Sukkah 31a).
but after the festival. If he claimed it from him after Sukkot.
and did not build it with mortar. For if he joined it with mortar it is judged a permanent structure and has the law of a beam built into a building (Rashi there).
it changed, he pays its value. As explained below chapter 2.

he must pay only the principal. Unlike a thief, who pays a fine if there are witnesses that he stole (Hilchot Genevah 1:4-6). And if he swore falsely and then admitted, he pays principal plus a fifth and brings a guilt offering (below 7:1-2).
and built it into the palace. Made it part of the palace, which is a large building.
since it did not change. Although now it is part of the building, nonetheless in itself it remains as it was.
even though he transgressed. The Torah prohibition of robbery.
it is not in the category of returning a robbed item. There is no commandment to return the robbed item.
bundles. Of vegetables and the like.
and the three of them are together worth two perutot and he returned two to him. So it turns out that he now holds a bundle worth less than a perutah.

there is robbery here but no commandment to return a robbed item here. He robbed the value of a perutah and became obligated to return it, but since less than a perutah of what he robbed remains in his hand, he is not obligated by the commandment of returning (the version before us in the Talmud, Bava Kamma 105a, reads: "there is no robbery here, and there is no commandment to return a robbed item here," and the Rishonim there brought several explanations; see the commentators who discussed the relationship between Maimonides' words here and this version).
in a settled place. An inhabited place.
lest it be seized from me here. For the wilderness is a place of danger and the robbed item is not safe with him.

and likewise with the value of the robbed item. In a case where he pays its value, the choice is the victim's not to receive the payment in the wilderness (see also Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 13:8, Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 7:11).
and slipped it to him in the account. When he settled accounts with the victim about another matter, he added the value of the robbed item into the account without his knowledge.

for a person tends to feel his purse at all times, etc.. A person is accustomed to check often how much money he has in his wallet, and one can assume that he already counted the coins that returned to him together with the other coins he had in his wallet.

and a count without knowledge discharges. Although the robber did not inform the owner that he had returned the money to his wallet, since the owner now knows that he has all his money, the robber is released from responsibility (compare Hilchot Genevah 4:10-11).

and if he returned it to a purse with nothing in it, he has not discharged. For he does not usually feel it at all times, and since he does not know that there is now money in it, he will not be careful to guard it.
and pressed him with friends and urged him until he took it from him. He sent his friends to persuade him to sell it to him until he finally agreed.
and one does not receive lashes for this negative commandment, for it involves no act. Since the prohibition is the urging of his fellow, and speech is not an act (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 18:1).

and he does not transgress this negative commandment until he takes the item he coveted. For although the essence of the prohibition of coveting is the urging, one does not transgress the prohibition if the coveting did not reach the stage of an act of actually acquiring the item.

once he thought in his heart how he might buy this thing from him and his heart was enticed by it, he transgressed a negative commandment. This speaks of one who thought how to obtain his desire, but mere desire alone is not included in the prohibition (see Eight Chapters of Maimonides, chapter 6).
and desire is only in the heart alone. Desire in itself is a mental act and not a practical one.
even though he offered them much money. That he offered them a high payment.

from the deed of Ahab and Naboth. Ahab, king of Israel, coveted the vineyard of Naboth the Jezreelite, and when Naboth would not agree to sell it to him, Ahab and Jezebel arranged to have him killed so that Ahab would receive the vineyard (I Kings, chapter 21).
"so are the ways of everyone greedy for gain; it takes away the life of its owners". Anyone who robs his fellow takes his life, even if only the value of a perutah.
it is an enactment of the Sages that they do not accept from him. One should not take the value of the robbed item from him.
in order to bring the upright path closer for the repentant. To ease matters for one who wants to return to the upright path (see also Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 4:5).

and even if the robber died and it is in the hands of his sons, it returns to its owners in kind. And this is not considered a change of possession that acquires together with despair (below 5:3). As for the obligation of the sons of a robber who died to return when the robbed item no longer exists, see below 5:5-6.
he acquired it by the change. And he does not need to return the robbed item itself, but pays the victim its value.
and pays its value as at the time of the robbery. According to what it was worth when it was robbed.
by oral tradition. The tradition of the Sages in the interpretation of the verses.
the robber acquired all the improvement that it improved after despair. As explained below 5:6.
rabbinically, for the sake of the repentant. The Sages enacted that the robber acquire the improvement after despair in order to make it easier for him to return the robbed item.
the buyer acquired it through despair and change of possession. And the same law applies to a thief (see Hilchot Genevah 5:3).

one who robs and improves and sells or bequeaths before despair, etc.. The robber himself acquires only the improvement after despair, but if he sold or bequeathed the robbed item, the buyer or heir acquires the improvement even without despair, and this is an enactment of the Sages (see Bava Kamma 96a).

and the victim returns and takes the value of the improvement from the robber, for he had not despaired. Between the robber and the victim the law remains that he does not acquire improvement made before despair, and therefore the victim collects from the robber the value of the improvement that he paid to the heir or buyer.

and likewise if the buyer or heir improved it, etc.. When the buyer or heir themselves improved the robbed item, they acquire the improvement even if the owners had not despaired, and the victim collects the improvement from the robber.
even if the gentile improved it, it returns to its owners. And he does not pay the gentile for improvement, for the gentile is not included in this enactment (Bava Kamma 96a).

the gentile sold it to a Jew after improving it... and if the victim seized it, we do not take it from his hand. This case was not decided in the Gemara (there), and because of the doubt we do not take money from one who holds it. But if the victim seized the improvement we do not take it from him, since he is now the one in possession.
we have already explained. Above halachot 1-2, and compare Hilchot Genevah 1:11-12.
and it grew. It grew wool.
he pays as at the time of the robbery. He returns the robbed item and the victim pays him for the improvement.
he pays the value of a cow about to give birth and the value of a ewe about to be sheared. And he acquired the offspring and the fleece because they came after despair.

it is still in its owners' possession even though the robber is liable for its accidents. Although the robber is liable for every accident and bears full responsibility like an owner, he does not have the law of an owner.
and consecrated. The animal as an offering.

and slaughtered after the owners despaired. After the consecration the owners despaired and then he slaughtered the animal outside the Temple (Mirkevet HaMishneh, which resolves the Raavad's objection in his critical notes).

it is in the robber's possession only from the moment he consecrated it, etc.. In Hilchot Ma'aseh HaKorbanot (18:14) it is explained that if he stole or robbed an animal and consecrated it and after despair slaughtered it outside, he is liable to karet like one who slaughters sacred offerings outside. And although it is not possible to consecrate something that is not one's own before despair, it is explained there that the Sages placed it in his possession in order to be strict with him so that he is liable to karet for slaughtering sacred offerings outside. And here it is explained that placing the animal in the robber's possession is from the time of the consecration onward and not already from the time of the robbery, so that he not gain the improvement from then (Mirkevet HaMishneh and Yad Peshutah).

if it was lean and he fattened it, even before despair he takes from the victim the improvement of the fattening. Some explained that this law too is for the sake of the repentant, that for improvement on which he spent money they enacted that he acquire it even before despair (Or Sameach and others; and see Even HaEzel, Nizkei Mamon 7:12, who explained differently; and compare Hilchot Genevah 1:11).
to its original state. To its initial state before it changed.
they return to being boards. They return to being wooden boards.
he must grind. Crumble.
a tongue. A raw piece.
he must return it to being a tongue. He must return it to being a tongue.
and planed them. Smoothed and polished them.
or dug in them. Carved in them to make them into containers or to carve another part of the vessel.
he beat it. Struck its fibers to separate them.
and whitened it. Cleaned it.
spun. Spun threads ready for weaving a garment.
and made it dust. Crumbled it.
and polished them and renewed them. Smoothed their surface and cleaned them.
they become dull. They become covered with a dark layer.
he robbed an attached palm tree and cut it down, he did not acquire it. Since its name was and remained a palm tree (Bava Kamma 96a).

he cut it into sections and made it into beams, he acquired. For this is a complete change, but if he merely cut it down and chopped it into sections and did not make beams of them, he did not acquire, because these are sections of a palm tree and not something else entirely (there).
if he cut them into boards until their name changed, he acquired. If he cut the beam into planks, this is a complete change.
he robbed leaves and made them into broom. He split the palm leaves into two parts in each leaf and made it into a sort of broom (Rashi, Bava Kamma 96a).
he robbed a lamb and it became a ram. He robbed a small lamb and kept it until it grew up and became a ram.
this is a change in his possession and he acquired it. Although he did not do an act with his hands, a substantive change occurred in the robbed item and he acquired it.
he robbed a vessel and broke it, we do not assess for him the depreciation. He cannot return the broken vessel and pay only the loss in value of the vessel according to the assessors' estimate.

for this is an enactment for the owners. And therefore although the vessel was broken or depreciated and a change was made in it, the robber did not acquire the item (and see the Gra, section 354 subsection 13, and Ketzot HaChoshen there subsection 3, who found difficulty in this; and compare Hilchot Genevah 1:15).
and became more expensive. It rose in price.

but the improvement of the price rise, if the robbed item exists, returns in kind. As for acquiring the improvement of the price rise when the robbed item no longer exists, see the beginning of the next chapter.
and it became more expensive with him and stood at four. It rose in price without any change occurring in it and its price stood at four dinars.

if he broke the jar, etc.. In principle the robber pays for the robbed item according to its value at the time of the robbery (Mishnah Bava Kamma 9:1), but when he destroyed it with his hands he pays according to its value at that time (see Bava Metzia 43a).
a wrapper. A covering, like a bag or box, made of palm leaves and the like, in which fresh dates are sold (Commentary on the Mishnah, Kelim 16:5).
and when he sells them one by one he sells for ten. If he sells the dates separately he will receive ten coins for them.
and the victim cannot say to him, I would have sold them one by one. And therefore the value of the robbed item is ten.
and the same law applies to one who damages. Also in a case where he damaged his fellow's property we assess the damage in the same way.

and likewise anything similar to this with ordinary property, but with consecrated property it is not so, rather he pays ten. For an ordinary person the Sages were lenient to assess by the overall value, since we find that the Torah was lenient in a similar matter in monetary damages (see Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 4:13 and the explanation there), but with consecrated property they were not lenient (see Bava Metzia 99b).
it grew lean. It became thin, weakened.
for example, illnesses that have no cure. That have no remedies that would help them.
or the king invalidated it. Who decreed that the coin could not be used for payment.
this is like one who robbed a vessel and broke it, etc.. And the robber takes the robbed item and pays the victim its full value (see above 2:15).
and it is accepted in another country. It can be used for payment in another place.
or terumah and it became impure. And it is forbidden to eat.
chametz and Pesach passed over it. And it became forbidden for eating and benefit.
an animal on which a transgression was committed. For example, it was mated with by a person and was disqualified from being offered.
or that was disqualified from being offered. For example, a blemish developed in it.
or that was going out to be stoned. And it is forbidden for benefit, such as an ox that killed a person.
he must return its value as at the time of the robbery. And not according to its value when it was lost, as explained above 5:2.

therefore, etc.. Since he must pay if it is lost, it turns out it still has value even though it is forbidden for benefit, and therefore if he denied the robbery and swore about it, he must pay its value plus a fifth and a guilt offering (as below 7:1).
even though he transgressed a negative commandment. Of robbery (above 1:3).

we penalize him, even outside the Land. Although ordinarily judges outside the Land do not judge fines and do not even collect fines enacted by the Sages (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 5:8-9), in exceptional cases it is permitted to act by emergency measure outside the ordinary law and to penalize one who breaks through the fences of religion or behaves violently (see there 24:6).
and we assess the wages or the improvement that he improved in the animal. We estimate how much the robber gained or how much his property improved because of the work.
the one who seizes. Holds by force.
he is exempt, for a person is pleased that his slave not be idle. Even though the slave becomes thin from the work, the slave's owner prefers this to an idle slave (Bava Kamma 97a).
if it is not made for hire. If the owner is not accustomed to rent it out.

if he went down to it in the manner of renting, etc.. That he intended to pay rent. In this case he can be judged as a renter who must pay rent, or as a robber (like one who borrows without knowledge, below halachah 15) who pays the depreciation, and therefore the owner of the ship will choose what to collect from him.
even though this resident is accustomed to rent a place for himself. That the resident is accustomed to rent a place for himself to live in.
for this one benefits and this one does not lose. The owners do not lose because of the resident's benefit, and therefore he does not have to pay them.
even though this one is not accustomed to rent. And it turns out that the resident does not gain by not paying rent for the courtyard.
and soaked dyes. Dyeing materials soaked in water separately from the wool.

he pays him the value of what he lost in the wool, etc.. When they assess the value of the dyed wool that the robber returns to the victim, the robber is at a disadvantage: if the value of the dyed wool decreased because of the dyeing he pays the difference, since he damaged the wool; and if the wool improved because of the dyes on it, he does not pay for what it improved (see Mirkevet HaMishneh).

and if the injured party seized the value of what was lacking from the dyes, we do not take it from his hand. For besides returning the wool, the robber must return the dyes. But there is a doubt about this whether returning the dyed wool is also considered returning the dye he took, or not. Therefore the court does not obligate him to pay for the dye, but if the owner seized the value of the dye from the dyer's property, we do not take it from his hand.
one who lays a hand on a deposit. He took the deposit that was deposited with him in order to bring it into his possession as a robber.

by means of his son, his slave and his agent, he is a robber and is liable for its accidents. Although ordinarily there is no agent for a transgression, with laying a hand the Sages learned that the agent's act binds the one who sent him (Kiddushin 42b).
he is not liable for its responsibility. As a robber; rather his law is still that of a guardian.
but he took the deposit... in order to lay a hand on it. That he brought it into his possession as a robber.
he became liable for its accidents. Of the jar and all the wine in it, since he lifted the whole jar.
the purse. A wallet.
and anything like a purse of things that are not one body. A container with several separate things in it that he lifted and intends to take only one thing from it.
this is a doubt. Perhaps only with a jar is he liable for all the wine because all the wine is one unit, and not in lifting a purse in which each dinar stands by itself.
it is in its owners' possession. And its law remains that of a deposit.
for he did not lift the jar. And the jar did not pass into his responsibility.

and if it turned sour he pays the value of all of it. If the wine remaining in the jar turned sour he is liable, since removing the revi'it of wine can cause the rest to turn sour (Commentary on the Mishnah, Bava Metzia 3:12).
and one of them took it and used it. One person took the item from them and used it.
until he returns it to the owners. And it is not enough that he return it to the one he took it from.

one who seizes a pledge from the hand of the borrower without the court's authorization. But a court agent is permitted to take the pledge by force from the borrower, provided he does not enter his house (see Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 3:4).

the Sages imposed a fine on robbers, etc.. And the reason for the fine is "so that damages and lawlessness among people do not multiply" (Commentary on the Mishnah, Shevuot 7:3, and compare Hilchot Chovel u-Mazik 5:4).
one who entered his fellow's house to take a pledge. And it is known that he entered for this purpose, and since it is forbidden to take a pledge by force he is treated as a robber (above 3:16).
under his wings. Under the wings of his garment.

the homeowner swears while holding an object. While holding a Torah scroll (Hilchot Shevuot 11:8, and see there halachah 11), according to the law of those who swear and take (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:2).
where he claimed things that he is presumed to have. That it is plausible that the claimant had such things in his possession.
for it is presumed that such things as he claimed are deposited with him. That it is plausible that such things are given to him for safekeeping.

even if he said, "I never entered," since he contradicts the witnesses, he is exempt. Although it was shown by the witnesses that he lied about his entering the house, he is not established as a liar regarding his claim that he did not take vessels from the house.
he swears the heset oath. A light oath (without holding an object) that the Sages imposed on a defendant in cases where he is exempt from a severe oath (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:3).

for it is possible that he entered to rob and did not rob. And therefore the fact that he entered to take a pledge does not testify that he actually took vessels from his house, and they did not enact that the claimant swear and take.
there was one witness testifying that he entered. For example, he testifies that he entered to take a pledge (Maggid Mishneh), which is forbidden as robbery (see above 3:16).
since the witness does not know what was under his wings. For if he had known, he would have obligated him to take the Torah oath (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:1).

for he is not established as a robber except by two witnesses. Since the Sages' enactment that he swears and takes when it is not known how much he took is based on his having been established as a robber, if there is only one witness that he took, he was not established as a robber, and the claimant does not swear and take.
just as the homeowner swears and takes. When there are witnesses that he robbed and it is not known what he took.

so too the homeowner's guardian. Who guards for the homeowner. And his law is not that of a witness but of the homeowner himself, and after he swears how much he took, the homeowner collects from the robber.

even the guardian's wife. For the deposit was given to the guardian with the understanding that his wife and household could also serve as guardians (see Hilchot She'elah u-Fikadon 4:8-9), and therefore she too can swear.
he was there. In the victim's house at the time of the robbery.
his hired worker. A temporary worker.

they do not swear and take. For it is doubtful whether they too are considered entrusted with guarding the house, and therefore it is doubtful whether their oath is effective, and money cannot be taken on their word.

and we do not make the robber swear because he is suspect regarding oaths. Since he is established as a robber, he is suspected of swearing a false oath and we do not make him swear (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 2:2).

the homeowner pronounces a general ban. By enactment of the Geonim, in certain cases where a person suspects another of claiming falsely against him and cannot obligate him to an oath, he can impose a ban (curse) in general on anyone who lies against him in that matter without mentioning the suspect's name (see Hilchot Sheluchin ve-Shutafin 3:11, Maggid Mishneh, Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:4).

and even if the robber admitted that he robbed part, he returns only the part he admitted. And he is not liable for the oath of one who admits part, since he is liable for it only in a definite claim.
this too is a fine, etc.. Compare Hilchot Mechirah 20:3.
he swears the heset oath like any defendant. See above 5:4 for explanation.
the Torah oath... like anyone who admits part. The oath by the Torah that a defendant is obligated to take when he admitted part of the sum the claimant claimed (Hilchot To'en ve-Nitan 1:1).
for he was not established as a robber by witnesses. And therefore he is not suspect regarding the oath.
even though he admitted that he took a pledge without authorization. And transgressed the prohibition of robbery (above 3:16).

since there are no witnesses there... he swears and collects his debt from the pledge. For if there are witnesses that he took it he must return the pledge even if it is known that the borrower owes him (Hilchot Malveh ve-Loveh 3:4).

for the mouth that forbade is the mouth that permitted. Just as the reason to obligate him is based on his statement that he took the vessels, so one can rely on his claim that he took them for his debt in order to exempt him.
as will be explained in Hilchot To'en. 1:2.
and even though this homeowner was accustomed to sell his vessels. And taking out the vessels in itself does not arouse suspicion.

for anyone who enters his fellow's house not in his presence and takes vessels from there... is presumed a robber. And therefore he is not believed even though the manner of taking the vessels is not suspicious (and compare Hilchot Genevah 5:12, where in the opposite situation, when a person took in the presence of the homeowner, he is believed, unless there is a combination of several suspicious circumstances).
and there is no oath here. The homeowner does not need to swear what was taken from him.
and after he returns it he returns and claims, etc.. If he still insists that he took them lawfully, he can sue the homeowner in a separate case.
and a high stone was outside Jerusalem. It was called Even HaToen (the Stone of the Claimant) (Bavli Bava Metzia 28b), and there they made the announcements, as detailed below in halachah 8.

and he need not be concerned because he announced the type of the lost object. He need not worry that by announcing what kind of lost object he found, a deceiver will come and claim that he lost this item and try to extract it from him by giving signs.
distinguishing signs. See below, halachah 5.
and the deceiver. A person who is presumed to be a deceiver.
and it shall be with you until your brother seeks it. They derived from the verse that the finder must keep the lost object until he inquires into and examines the one who claims it is his.
once deceivers multiplied etc.. When fraudulent claimants multiplied, they decreed that everyone is suspected of deception until he proves he is not a deceiver.

and they rule on their basis everywhere by Torah law. These signs are considered full proof, and they are relied upon by Torah law and not merely by virtue of a rabbinic decree (Bavli Bava Metzia 28a). They are relied upon in other matters as well (see, for example, Hilchot Gerushin 3:11).
measure, weight, number, or the place of the lost object are distinguishing signs. For examples of signs that are not distinguishing, see below 18:7.
he gives it to the one with the witnesses. Witnesses' testimony that the object belongs to a particular person takes precedence over signs.
a single witness is as if there were none. A single witness has no legal force for presenting proof, so it comes out as signs against signs.
he gives it to those who testify to its falling. Since it is possible that it was woven for the first person and, after he sold it, it fell from the buyer.
he stated its weights. He said what its weight is.
he gives it to the one who stated its weight. Because it is less noticeable to the eye.
the imriyot. Threads at the edge of the garment.
he would announce it for three festivals. In Jerusalem.
on the first festival he says 'first'. When he announces, he informs that this is the first festival on which he is announcing it.
so that 'second' will not be confused for him with 'third'. Lest the owner mistakenly hear 'second' and think he has one more festival to give signs.
within seven days. During the seven days after the festival (Peirush HaMishnah, Bava Metzia 2:6).
so that the listener can go to his house etc.. So that even one who lives far away can return and give signs.
and this finder will find the announcer announcing on the seventh. He will find the announcer in the announcement of the seventh day.
after the Temple was destroyed. And there was no single central place for announcements.

after oppressors multiplied and said, 'The lost object belongs to the king'. For the king acted unlawfully, and they feared people who would force him to give them the lost object on the king's behalf (Peirush HaMishnah, Bava Metzia 2:6).
they decreed. The Sages decreed.
until Elijah comes. An expression whose practical meaning is that the situation remains as it is until the matter is clarified.
it was lost through circumstances beyond his control. He cannot return it intact because of an event beyond his control.
like a paid guardian. A guardian for payment (Hilchot Sechirut 1:2).
because he is engaged in a mitzvah. He is taking care of the lost object.
and he is exempted from several positive commandments etc.. For example, giving charity to a poor person while he is taking care of it, and this is his reward (Bavli Bava Kamma 56b).
to inspect. To supervise.
a woolen garment, he shakes it out. So that it does not become spoiled by moths, but a linen garment he should not touch (Peirush HaMishnah, Bava Metzia 2:8).
and he may not shake it out with a stick. By means of a stick.
nor with two people. Holding it from its two sides, out of concern that they will stretch it excessively.
for its need. So that it will be aired out.
but not by fire, because it wears them down. For fire wears them down.
rakes. Implements for raking.
and axes. A kardom, a kind of hatchet used for splitting wood.
he may use them with a soft material. With a soft substance that does not damage them.
he may not touch them. Since they are preserved even without use.

and just as they said regarding a lost object, so they said regarding a deposit whose owners went overseas. He may use it in the manner described here so that it is preserved, and this is because of the mitzvah of returning lost objects. But if the owners are in the same land as the guardian, he may not touch it (Hilchot She'elah U'Pikadon 7:4).
books. Books written on parchment or paper rolled as a scroll, which need to be aired.
initially. First-time study.
and he may review. He may read it a second time.

and he may not read a passage and translate it. According to the custom of translating the passage in parallel with the reading (Hilchot Tefillah 12:10). The reason in these cases is that he uses the book more than is necessary to preserve it and may damage it slightly.
pages. Columns.
topics. Subjects.

he appraises their value and puts them on. He assesses and estimates their worth, so that he will know how to repay the owner the value of the tefillin, and afterward he may put on the tefillin and use them for himself.
because it is a thing readily available to everyone. Tefillin are something that can be readily bought.
and they are made only for their mitzvah. See the Piskei V'Shitot.
for he must feed it. And the owner must bear this expense (below, halachah 19).
that it does. Work.
and he hires them out. Rents them out for payment.
and if their rental income exceeds. The cost of feeding them.
from here on he appraises their value on himself etc.. The finder assesses their worth, and in exchange for caring for the animal going forward he becomes a partner in the profits with the owner.

like the law of anyone who appraises an animal from his fellow. One who cares for an animal in exchange for a share of the profits, with its value first appraised so that it will be known at the end how much it improved (Hilchot Sheluchin V'Shutafin 8:1-3).
calves and foals. Which are small and do not work like a cow or a donkey.
of pasture. That eat at pasture.
and of fattening. From the word for health, as they are meant for fattening and the cost of caring for them is higher.
are given to the finder. To look after them.
that a raiding band seized. That were taken by soldiers.

they are with him like a loan. They are lent to him. In contrast to the guardian of a lost object, who has the law of a paid guardian and is exempt for circumstances beyond his control, in this case, where he may use the money, he becomes like a borrower who must pay even for circumstances beyond his control.
with the proceeds of the lost object. With the money he received from selling the lost object.
but money found as a lost object. If he found money.
for he is a paid guardian. And is liable only for theft and loss, and exempt for circumstances beyond his control.
as we have explained. Above, halachah 10.
from his own. From his own money and not from their earnings.
for the sake of the betterment of the world. As explained in the next halachah.
he leaves the lost object and goes. And refrains from returning the lost object.
a purse. A wallet.

and the owner of the lost object claimed that there were two purses tied together etc.. It follows from his claim that apparently the finder separated them, and now he returns only one and claims that this is how he found it.

the garment was included in 'any lost object of your brother'... why did the verse specify etc.. The verses command returning every lost object, yet they also specify several particular items that must be returned. The Sages noted that these are already included in the general command, and explained that each one comes to teach an additional detail in these laws.
a mardaat. A kind of blanket used as a saddle for carrying loads.
something subordinate to it. That the mardaat is subordinate to the donkey itself.
such as a single nail etc.. But if he found two or more, their number is considered a sign (below 16:1).
or a single coin etc.. The markings of the coin itself are not considered a sign (below, halachah 10), but when he finds coins gathered together, their number is considered a sign (below 16:2).
for their mind is set on giving the signs that it has and getting it back. They rely on being able to get their lost object back after they tell the finder its signs.
woe for the lack in the purse. This is an expression of grief over the loss of money.
and similar statements that show they despaired. Other ways that indicate they gave up hope.
in the sea or in the river. Above 11:10.
or in a place where most are non-Jews. Above 11:7.
but if the owners are still saying. Mistakenly.
in the cabinet. A wall cupboard.
perhaps I erred in the count. Even if he counted it with other things and the total is short, he may think he miscounted and has not yet despaired.
and he did not know of it. He did not know that it fell from him.
and took the dinar. The one who saw it took it for himself.
as we have explained. Above 11:2.
this is a gift. As if he had given him a gift.
and after despair, he intended to rob him of it. To take it for himself.
he transgressed 'you shall surely return them'. But there is no prohibition of robbery in this, since they had already despaired of it.
he waited for it. He lingered and did not take it.
for they had despaired, as we have explained. Above, halachah 2.

he transgresses only 'you may not ignore them'. Above 11:1 it says that if he left and did not return the lost object, he also nullified the positive commandment of 'you shall surely return them.' Some explained that in the case stated here, where he lingered there until the owners despaired and he was released from the obligation to return, the failure to return is not due to him, and it is not he who nullified the mitzvah (Ran, Bava Metzia 30a, cited in Avnei Ezel).
he saw a sela or a coin that fell. For example, where the owner knew that the coin fell from him.
even from three people. One might have thought that the owner despaired because he thinks one of them will take the coin and claim that it was not he who found it but his fellow.
even though it is not worth a perutah to each one. It is worth less than three perutot, and there is no mitzvah of returning a lost object worth less than a perutah (above 11:12).
perhaps they are partners. And for that reason they rely on each other that if they find the coin they will return it, and so they do not despair.

and one of them waived his share to his fellow etc.. One gave up his share to his fellow, so it follows that it is worth a perutah to each of the remaining partners (based on Bavli Bava Metzia 26b and Rashi there).
and it disappeared from him. It vanished from his sight.
this is like something that fell into the sea. Above, halachah 4.
a sieve. A strainer.
with a weak mind. A weak attitude.
the searchers. People who are accustomed to search for things.
for the markings of the coin are not a sign. The markings of the coin itself, but he may give another sign, such as that they were placed in a certain arrangement (below 16:2).
for its presumption is that it is spent. A coin is presumed to be something that leaves its owner's possession in commerce, and he does not hold it back.
one who finds an item with no sign next to an item that has a sign. It is possible that they were lost together (Bavli Bava Metzia 25a); see below 15:13-14.
the owner of the sign. The owner of the lost object that has a sign on it.
that the eye has become accustomed to them. That through frequent use he can recognize them without a specific sign.
a vatik. One who is careful to act properly (above 5:10).
who does not deviate at all in his speech. From the truth.
in Mikva'ot. Tractate Mikva'ot.
and said, 'In this one I sleep,' lest semen be found there. He says that he sleeps in a different bed lest a seminal emission be found, and this is a disgrace.
so that they would not trouble the one who hosted him. If it becomes known that Shimon is willing to host in his home, more people will come to stay with him, causing him trouble.
and he added and subtracted. From the truth when speaking with one about the other (see Hilchot De'ot 5:7).
if he found it in the manner of placement. In a way that shows it was deliberately placed in that spot (though it is possible that the owner forgot it there after placing it).
it is forbidden to return it there. For the owner will come to search for it there and not find it.

and any item that has a sign, whether in the manner of placement... he must announce. If he transgressed and took it (Maggid Mishneh), for initially one should not touch something found in the manner of placement.
a covered vessel in a refuse heap. And apparently it was hidden there deliberately.

as it says 'strayed'. The verse says: “You shall not see your brother's ox or his sheep strayed and ignore them; you shall surely return them to your brother,” implying that only something strayed and lost from its owner must be returned, but if it was left there deliberately, it is not lost.
a donkey and its equipment. The equipment on it, such as the saddle.
and a cow running among the vineyards. In such a situation the cow itself may be harmed by the vineyard, and therefore it is defined as a lost object (Bavli Bava Metzia 31a).
at night. For their way is to be with their owners then.
toward the end of the day. Near sunset.
and at twilight. Before sunrise.
if he saw them for three days etc.. For three consecutive days, presumably they were lost. But in less than that, it is possible that once or twice they went out to graze early or delayed returning.
a loss of land. That the cow damages the vineyards (above 11:20).
if the vineyards belonged to a non-Jew, it is not a lost object and he need not return it. For the lost object of a non-Jew is permitted in principle (above 11:3).
and if he feared that the non-Jew might kill it... it is a lost object. For the cow itself is in danger of being lost to its owner.
in the public domain. In a place used by the public.
beyond the boundary. At a distance of more than two thousand cubits from the city.
he must return it. For presumably it will lose its way.
among the grasses. A grazing place.
in a pen that does not guard. From which it can leave if it wishes.
and it is not causing it to be lost. It does not cause the cow to leave.
he may not touch it, for this is not a lost object. Rather it is there with the owner's knowledge.
an axe. A kind of hatchet.

he may not touch them. For this is not a lost object (Bavli Bava Metzia 31a), such as where they are placed in a guarded place or where it is the workers' practice to leave their belongings there (Tosafot there 25b).
on the highway. A main road.
the gate. The gate of an area enclosed by partitions.

he may not touch them, lest their owners placed them there etc.. It is uncertain whether they were deliberately placed there or whether they were stolen from elsewhere and are lost. Their law is that of a doubtful placement, which one should not take initially, and if he took it, it is his (above, halachah 1).

and if they were tied with a knot that is a sign, he must announce. Although in a case of doubtful placement one should initially not take it even if it has a sign (see above, halachah 1), it seems that here he may take it since the place is not entirely guarded (Derishah, Choshen Mishpat 260:11).
he found them fixed in their place. That were not stolen.
for the place is a sign. The location of the lost object can be given as a sign.
as we have explained. Above, halachah 2.
and he changed his mind. He regretted it.
and he changed his mind about it to clear it out... he takes and announces. So that it will not be lost to its owner.
and even if they were covered in a fixed refuse heap, he takes and announces. Since they are small, it is possible they were thrown there by mistake along with other things.
he found scattered fruit. And they have no sign.

and likewise if he found small bundles of sheaves in the public domain, for they have no sign. In this case he may take the bundles even if they were found in the manner of placement (compare below, halachah 10). The Gemara explains (Bavli Bava Metzia 23a) that since the bundles roll about in the public domain, their having been placed has no significance.
rounds of dried figs. Pressed dried figs in the shape of a circle.
and the loaves of a baker. A baker who makes loaves in a uniform mold.
and strings of fish. Fish strung on a cord.
and fleeces of wool coming from their country. Fleeces from their places of growth, not yet processed.
and bundles of flax. Packages of flax.
and tongues of purple wool. Combed wool dyed purple.

for a sign that is liable to be trampled is still a sign. Even though the sign can be trampled and ruined by passersby, since it is not certain that it will be trampled, the owners may not have despaired.
loaves of a householder. Which are not uniform.
and fleeces of wool taken from the craftsman's house. For each craftsman processes them differently.
jars of wine and jars of oil. For each one has jars of a distinctive shape.
and if the storehouses of wine and oil were opened. If the owners of the wine and oil began selling the jars they had stored, in which case the shape of the jar does not indicate the owner.

even though they are marked. The marking is a seal of clay joining the lid of the jar to the jar itself, made at the time of purchase, and one might have thought it would serve as a sign for the owner.
for all the jars are marked this way etc.. The manner of sealing is similar in all jars, so the marking is not considered a sign.
if in the manner of falling, they are his. For they have no sign.
and if in the manner of placement, he must announce. For presumably they were placed there and forgotten.
the place is a sign. For in a private domain they do not usually roll about under people's feet (Bavli Bava Metzia 23a).

even though it is not a distinguishing sign. Although above 13:5 it says that a place is a distinguishing sign, in the case stated here it is not certain that the place serves as a sign, as there is concern that the bundles moved from their place. In any event he announces, because it is possible that they stayed in place and the owner will give a sign regarding the place (Kesef Mishneh, and see Yad Peshutah).
sheaves. Bundles of ears of grain larger than small bundles.
he takes and announces. Because of their weight they stay in place and the place is considered a sign.
a round. Of dried figs, above, halachah 8.
a shard. A piece of pottery.
for it is unusual in its cut. For it is cut in a different shape than usual.
in the place of the threshing floors. A place where the harvest is gathered.
like a kav within four cubits. If there is a kav of fruit in an area of four cubits by four cubits.
because the owners do not trouble themselves to gather them. Because of their scattering.
lest the owners placed them there. And they intend to return and gather them, since they are not completely scattered.
if they were like half a kav etc.. If the quantity of fruit and the area of scattering differ, but in the same ratio of quantity to area.

half a kav in two cubits. On one hand the fruit is scattered over a smaller area and is easier to gather, but on the other hand there is a smaller quantity of fruit and perhaps the owners would not want to trouble themselves for such an amount.
or two kavs in eight cubits. There is a large quantity of fruit, but it is scattered over a larger area.

or if the kav was of two or three kinds etc.. There is a mixture of different kinds, some of which are small and hard to gather and some large and easy to gather, some of which are expensive and some cheap.
piles of fruit. A heap of fruit.

he found a vessel with fruit before it, they are his, the fruit and the vessel etc.. According to the text before us, this case concerns a vessel with no sign, and therefore both the vessel and the fruit belong to the finder. The commentators found this text difficult, since in the earlier cases it apparently speaks of a vessel that has a sign, so this one would too; therefore some emended it here to read “the fruit is his, and the vessel he takes and announces” (Maggid Mishneh, followed by recent printings, and accordingly the end of the sentence “for they have no sign” must also be emended, and so it is written in the Shulchan Aruch; and see also the Yalkut Shinuy Nusachot in the Frankel edition, who discussed the matter at length and tried to resolve the text as we have it).
before the fruit. Opposite the fruit.
the face of the vessel. The opening of the vessel.
we suspect that they spilled from the vessel. And he must announce.
agannim. The neck of the vessel or a bent-over rim (see Peirush HaMishnah, Keilim 25:6; Rashi, Niddah 3b).
because of the agannim. Which prevent them from coming out; compare Hilchot She'ar Avot HaTumot 17:1.
if some of the fruit was in the vessel and some on the ground, he must announce. Whether it has agannim or not.
ketzitzot. Detached fruit.
even next to a field of ketzitzot. And presumably they came from it.
and likewise a fig tree. A fig tree.
for a fig and the like becomes repulsive with its falling. The fig and the ketzitzot become too repulsive to eat once they fall to the ground, and the owners renounce them.
and exempt from tithes. Since he acquired them from ownerless property before their processing was complete, and ownerless property is exempt from tithes (see Hilchot Ma'aser 3:21).
but olives and carobs etc.. Which do not become repulsive when they fall, and therefore he does not renounce them.
for the owners renounced them to everyone. Because vermin and creeping things are found on them (Bavli Bava Metzia 22b).
and this is their presumption. It is presumed that they renounced them, and they are also exempt from tithes (Hilchot Ma'aser 13:1).
and if they belonged to orphans, who cannot renounce. And the renunciation of minor orphans has no force.
and he fenced in the place of the trees. With a fence or the like.
or prepared the place. Readied it.
the novelot. Dates that fall from the tree.
it is forbidden to keep it. One may not hold on to it.
and there is no obligation of returning a lost object in it. If it was lost, he is not obligated to return it.
even though its hide is useful. Even though its hide has value and its owners lose it.
rather anyone who finds it acquires it. Compare Hilchot Nizkei Mamon 13:14.
a fledgling etc.. That hops but does not yet fly, and therefore does not stray far from its dovecote (see Hilchot Shevitat Yom Tov 2:6).
found between two dovecotes. And both are within fifty cubits.
half and half. If the two dovecotes are equally near the fledgling.
one who finds needles etc.. And generally there is no sign on such small items.
and hooks. A kind of hook or barb used for various things.
for the number is a sign. The number of items in a lost object is considered a sign (above 13:5).
a pile of coins. Many coins gathered together.

or some of them were on some of the others, such that if he inserts a splinter between them they would all be lifted at once. Each coin lies on the one beneath it, such that if one were to push a stick under the bottom coin, they could be lifted together.
he must announce. For they were certainly placed and did not fall.
like a row. Placed in a circle.
like a chatzuvah. That has three legs.
like a line. Side by side.
like a ladder. Possibly it means placed at some distance from one another like the rungs of a ladder (according to Rabbeinu Chananel).
this is a doubt. Whether they were placed deliberately or fell.
in a purse. A wallet.
or a purse as it is. Empty.
and if the circumstances show... he must announce. Compare above 15:13.
a counter. The table placed between the shopkeeper and the customers.
and if he found them on the counter, they belong to the finder. Because the shopkeeper does not leave money there, and presumably one of the customers left it there.
from the counter outward. On the customers' side.
and why should the shop not acquire it for the shop owner. For a person's domain acquires on his behalf under the law of the courtyard acquisition.
he must say, 'Let my shop acquire it for me'. And it is not enough that he is standing there.
as will be explained. Below 17:8.
the money changer. A changer who exchanges coins.
stool. The money changer's table.
bundled. Gathered in a bundle.
provided that most are non-Jews. Only if most of the people in that place are non-Jews does he acquire the bundle.
as we have explained. Above 11:7.
where the fruit came from the merchant. A trader who buys goods and sells them to others, and it is not known from whom they fell, and since they have no sign he need not announce.
or through his Canaanite slaves and maidservants. For their property belongs to their owners (Hilchot Malveh V'Loveh 2:8), and what fell from them is as if it fell from the householder.
he must return it. To the householder, for the money certainly fell from him.
in a heap. A pile of stones from a building that collapsed.
they belong to the ancient non-Jews. Who were there in the past, and their lost property is ownerless.
lest they were placed there. By a Jew, and something doubtful as to whether it was placed may not be touched (above 15:1).
as will be explained. Below 17:8.
Amorites. The Amorite people who lived in the past in the land of Canaan.
and if a person's lost object etc.. Which is his, and yet when it is lost from him and from everyone, it belongs to the finder (see above 11:10).
and found. And readily available.
he found a treasure in a new wall. In a hole that goes through from both sides, and since the wall is new it is clear that it was not placed by ancient non-Jews.
its handle proves it. The handle of the knife, which faces the side of the one who hid it.
and the purse, its mouth proves it. The opening of the purse also faces the side of the one who hid it (Peirush HaMishnah, Bava Metzia 2:3).
and if the inside of the wall was found full of them. With many items of the treasure, and there is no proof from which side they were inserted (see Yad Peshutah).
they divide. The finder and the householder.
for there is nothing there that proves it. There is no proof from the manner of placement from which side it was placed.
from its middle outward. In the outer half of the thickness of the wall.
from its middle inward. In the inner half of the thickness of the wall.
or if he was an heir. If the householder died and his rights passed to the heir.
for we make claims on his behalf. Because perhaps he is not familiar with his father's affairs and would lose out because of it (see Hilchot Sanhedrin 7:9).
they belong to the last renter. For everyone before him took what he had hidden before leaving.
and if he rented it to three non-Jews. But if he rented it to three Jews, it does not become an inn and he must return it (and its law is as above 14:8, Maggid Mishneh).
an inn. A lodging for travelers.
and anything found in it, even inside the house. Whether it was not hidden or was hidden inside.
for he has made it an inn. It is thus a public place, and its law is like a shop and a money changer (above, halachot 4-5).
or to his domain. For example his courtyard, below, halachah 8.
and another came and took possession of it. Performed an act of acquisition on it.
the one who took possession of it acquired it. Because an act of acquisition must be performed on a found object, and seeing a found object or falling upon it is not an act of acquisition.
once he lifted it for him. For movable property is acquired by lifting.

the rider acquired it even though it did not reach his hand. Since he said to his fellow, 'Acquire it for me,' he meant that he should perform an act of acquisition for him, and presumably he indeed lifted it for the rider and he acquired it immediately.
and if he said to him, 'Give it to me'. And the implication of his words is that he should hand the found object over to him and not acquire it for him.

and he took it for himself and said, 'I acquired it,' the taker acquired it. Since it did not come into the rider's hand, he did not acquire it, and it is in the hand of the one who lifted it, so he can acquire it.
and if after he gave it to the rider he said to him, 'I acquired it first,' he has said nothing. Since he gave it to the rider, presumably he did not intend to acquire it for himself.
and even though he said nothing to him. His fellow, but the one who lifted it intended on his own that his fellow would acquire by this lifting.
two lifted the found object. To acquire it for themselves.
both of them acquired it. And they divide the found object between them.

since they lack understanding. And therefore they are not capable of acquisition and gaining possession (unless they lifted it for themselves, in which case they acquire it by rabbinic law, as below, halachah 12).

a deaf-mute and a person of sound faculties lifted it together; since the person of sound faculties did not acquire, the deaf-mute did not acquire. When two people of sound faculties lift, they acquire together because each lifts his side on behalf of both. But if each lifts only for himself, they acquire nothing, because each lifts only part of the found object and partial lifting does not acquire at all. And in the case where a deaf-mute and a person of sound faculties lifted together, the deaf-mute cannot assist the person of sound faculties to acquire it with him, since a deaf-mute cannot acquire on behalf of others, and therefore the person of sound faculties also does not intend to lift on behalf of the deaf-mute, and neither of them acquires.

if both were deaf-mutes, both acquired; the Sages decreed that they acquire. By strict law neither acquires, as in the case of a deaf-mute and a person of sound faculties, but the Sages decreed that they gain possession.

so that they do not come to quarrel. To quarrel with others who would gain possession of it. But in the case of a deaf-mute and a person of sound faculties there is no such concern, because the deaf-mute sees that the person of sound faculties did not acquire either (Bavli Bava Metzia 8a).
and they led it. They guided it by speech or with a stick.
they pulled it. They grasped it and pulled it until it moved.
or if one was leading and one was pulling. Simultaneously.
both of them acquired. And they divide the animal, because both acts of acquisition are effective for an animal (Hilchot Mechirah 2:6).

the one who pulled acquired, but not the one who led. A camel is acquired by pulling or by leading, but pulling takes precedence over leading, so if one pulls and one leads, the one who pulls acquires it (Maggid Mishneh and Kesef Mishneh, and the Maggid Mishneh wrote that the Raavad's critique is based on an error in the version of the Rambam that he had).
and held the halter. He held the rope used for leading or tying the animal and did not pull it.
did not acquire. The animal.

and likewise with the property of a convert. A convert who has no children, and since he therefore has no heirs, after his death his property is ownerless and has the law of a found object (Hilchot Zechiyah U'Matanah 1:6).
but he acquired the halter alone. The part that is in his hand (Haggahot Maimoniyot, as below, halachah 7), for a person acquires what is in his hand without any further act of acquisition.

if one was riding and one was holding the halter etc.. If one rides and no one holds the halter, he acquires the animal and thereby acquires the whole halter, but if another holds the halter he prevents him from acquiring all of it, and each acquires what is with him and the rest remains ownerless.
and the rest of the halter. The part between his hand and the animal.
a person's courtyard etc.. See also Hilchot Zechiyah U'Matanah 4:8-9.
acquires for him without his knowledge. For his courtyard is like an agent who acquires on his behalf (below, halachah 10).
in a guarded courtyard. An item found in it is guarded, as if it were in the hand of an agent of the courtyard's owner.
they will quarrel. They will dispute.
a minor girl. Before she reaches the age of twelve and has brought signs of maturity (Hilchot Ishut 2:1).
and a minor boy. Before he reaches the age of thirteen and has brought signs of maturity (there, halachah 10).

we learned it from her hand. Regarding the giving of a get to a woman the Torah says “and he shall place it in her hand” (Deuteronomy 24:1), and the Sages learned that her courtyard is also like her hand (Hilchot Gerushin 5:1). A minor girl is included in this as well, since she too can be divorced by a get (there 2:19), and from the get they learned for other matters.
and the minor boy, since he cannot appoint an agent. Since he has no understanding, he cannot appoint an agent (Hilchot Sheluchin V'Shutafin 2:2).
for it is a broken-legged gazelle. Whose leg is broken.
fledglings that have not yet flown. That move slowly.
and if he were to run he would reach them etc.. Overtake them, and therefore they have the law of a lost object lying in the field.

since another transferred them to him etc.. Acquisition through transfer by the owner takes precedence over acquiring ownerless property, which depends only on himself, and therefore since they move and advance across the field they are considered placed in it, even if he cannot overtake them (Bavli Bava Metzia 12a). All this is provided that he stands beside his field and says, 'Let my field acquire it for me' (Hilchot Zechiyah U'Matanah 4:8-9).
there is robbery in it for the sake of peaceful ways. By strict law they do not acquire and it is permitted to take from them, but the Sages ruled that there is a prohibition of robbery in this.

therefore if another passed by and robbed it from their hands, it is not recovered through the courts. One cannot sue him in court for this, like the law of any robbery that is only rabbinic (above 6:16).

and if he denied it and swore, he is not liable for the fifth. If he robbed this found object and swore that he had not robbed, he does not pay the fifth as he would for an ordinary robbery (above 7:1-2), for one is not liable for a fifth for a rabbinic robbery (above 6:16).
those who are supported at his table. Who are fed by him.

even though they are adults. Although an adult has the capacity to acquire, the Sages decreed that his father acquires it, since he is supported by him and it is fitting that he give him what he finds (see Rashi, Bava Metzia 12b, and other Rishonim, that the reason is to avoid ill will).

and even if she was sold as a maidservant. She was sold as a maidservant by her father and lives in her master's house. Her found objects belong to him because the father is entitled to all money his daughter earns before she comes of age (Peirush HaMishnah, Bava Metzia 1:5; see also Hilchot Ishut 3:11, Hilchot Avadim 3:15).
and the found objects of his Canaanite slave and maidservant. For their property belongs to their owners (Hilchot Malveh V'Loveh 2:8).

and the found objects of his wife are his. The Sages awarded the husband her found objects out of concern for ill will, lest he say that he supports her from his own and she takes the found object for herself (Bavli Bava Metzia 12b; see also Hilchot Ishut 21:1).
for she is divorced and not divorced. Doubtfully divorced, and although she is not definitely divorced, nevertheless since he is going to divorce her, the reason of ill will does not apply.
even though it did not specify the liability of properties. The document does not state that the borrower accepts liability on his properties.

liability of properties. As security for repayment of the debt, the borrower may pledge his properties to the debt, so that if he sells some of his properties to another person and at the time of repayment cannot repay the debt, the lender can take them from the buyer (to 'seize from the purchasers') by virtue of the lien and collect from them (Hilchot Malveh V'Loveh 18:1).
and even though the debtor admits. That he did not repay the debt.
and even though it is validated. The signatures of the witnesses on the document were authenticated, and there is no concern that it is forged.

lest he paid it and they are colluding in order to seize from the purchasers unlawfully. There is concern that the debt was paid and the lender and borrower made a fraudulent agreement between them to claim that the debt was not paid, so that the lender would seize land the borrower sold and they would divide the money between them.

for the unspecified liability is a scribal error. The assumption is that in an ordinary debt the borrower accepts liability on his properties unless otherwise noted, and if the liability was not written in the document we attribute it to an error of the scribe who wrote it and treat the document as one that includes liability.
therefore if it was specified in this document that it is without liability. There is no concern of collusion, only that it was paid.
if the debtor admits, he returns it. For there is no concern that it was paid.
and likewise if he found a document dated that very day. That was written on the same day it was found.

and it was validated and the debtor admits, he returns it. In this case we do not suspect collusion, since it is unlikely that a person would repay on the day he borrowed, and presumably the debt is valid.

and if it is not validated, he does not return it, lest he wrote it to borrow and has not yet borrowed. Sometimes a borrower prepares promissory notes in advance although he has not yet borrowed, and when a document is found that is not validated it is quite possible that it is not validated because the loan has not yet been made. And even if the borrower admits that he borrowed, it is not returned in this case, since we are concerned that he did not really borrow but plans to borrow afterward, and only then would the lien take effect, so the document would be antedated, and he could unlawfully seize from buyers who bought land from the borrower between the date written in the document and the time the loan actually took place (see Sma, subsection 22, and see also Netivot HaMishpat).
in a skin bottle. A leather vessel.
he returns it to the one who gave a sign. On the vessel, which proves that the document fell from him.

he found three documents rolled together in one roll etc.. For example, all the documents have the same lender and borrower and it is not known from whom they fell (Maggid Mishneh; see the next halachah where there are differences among the documents).
placed one on another. He placed the end of each document over the end of the next and rolled them that way.
or bound in one bundle. He placed them whole one on top of the other and rolled them that way.
if the borrower was one and the lenders were three. If the borrower's name is the same in all the documents but the lender's name is different.

if they are validated, he returns them to the borrower. Since after validation each lender takes his document, it is not likely that they fell together from the lenders; rather it is more likely that the borrower paid them, and after they returned the documents to him they fell from him.
lest the lenders gave their documents to the scribe to validate them. In court.
and they fell from the judge's hand. In which case the documents were not paid.
he returns to the lender. And he need not give a sign (Shulchan Aruch). It is clear that they fell from him, since the names of the borrowers and the scribe's handwriting differ.

lest all three took their documents to the scribe to write. It is possible that before they borrowed, the borrowers brought the scribe papers to write documents on, and he wrote them and afterward they fell from him.
he found torn documents. And the tearing testifies that they were paid.
and a promissory note among them. That is not torn.

he does not return. Even though all the documents are from one lender, he does not return it to him, since it lies among torn documents it may also have been paid. On the other hand, he does not return it to the borrower, since there is no proof that this document was paid.
a receipt. A document in which the lender releases the borrower from the debt.
even without witnesses, he gives the promissory note to the borrower. Even though the receipt is not signed by witnesses, we follow it (compare Hilchot Malveh V'Loveh 16:9-10).
women's gittin. A bill of divorce.
when the husband admits. That he already divorced her with this get.

he gives it to the woman. This is provided that there is no concern that the get was written for another couple whose names are identical to the names of the man and woman before us (Maggid Mishneh, based on Hilchot Gerushin 3:9-11).
a distinguishing sign. Above 13:3.
for if it had not reached her hand she would not have known. But he could know in any case, since the get was originally with him, and therefore she has precedence over him.

he says it was lying in a skin bottle... it is given to him, for this is not a distinguishing sign. The fact that she knows this does not prove that it fell from her, since she knows where he keeps his belongings (Bavli Bava Metzia 28a, and therefore in an ordinary found object such a sign would be effective, as above, halachah 3).
he found a get of manumission. A document in which a master frees his slave.
when the master admits. That he already freed the slave.
a deed of gift. A document in which he transfers land as a gift.
if it is the gift of a healthy person. A gift from a healthy person, which cannot be retracted after the document has been given.
lest he wrote to give and did not give. It is possible that he wrote him the document but did not give it to him.
and after he wrote this document he sold this field or gave it as a gift to another and retracted. After the owner wrote the document he sold or gave the field to another person and regretted it.

and this one admits to that one in order to collude against the last one to whom he gave or sold. The owner admits that he gave the deed of gift to the first, so that the first will take it from the second, and then share it with the owner.

and if it is the gift of one on his deathbed. If the giver is a shechiv mera, that is, a sick person who has taken to his bed, whose gifts are governed by different laws than those of a healthy person (Hilchot Zechiyah U'Matanah 8:2).

for a person on his deathbed who gave to two, one after the other, the last one acquired. A deathbed gift takes effect only at the time of death, and therefore he can retract until death and give to another what he already gave. So when he admits that the deed of gift fell from the recipient, he is not colluding but is now giving him the land lawfully and cancelling the second gift.
as will be explained. Hilchot Zechiyah U'Matanah 9:15.

if the person on his deathbed died, having given it as a gift etc.. If at the time the document was found the person on his deathbed had already died, and it is his heir who admits that it fell from the recipient.
lest he wrote to give and did not give. Perhaps the person on his deathbed wrote the gift but did not give the document to the recipient.
and the heir sold it or gave it. After the person on his deathbed died and he inherited his property.
and he wants to collude with this one etc.. The heir admits that his predecessor gave the deed of gift, so that the recipient will take it from the second and they will share it between them.

he found a receipt. A document of release from a debt, and it is uncertain whether the debt was paid and the receipt was given to the borrower and fell from him, or the debt was not paid and it fell from the lender.
when the owner of the document admits that his document was cancelled and he was paid or forgave it. That his document is void because the debt was paid or he forgave it.
he gives it to the owner of the receipt. To the borrower for whom the receipt was written.
he found a ketubah... he does not return it to the woman. Like a promissory note that fell, above, halachah 1.
and he wants to collude against the purchasers. So that the woman will collect from the purchasers what he sold them after the ketubah was written.
igrot shum. When land of a borrower is collected, the court writes in the document which land will be collected, based on appraisers who valued land worth the amount of the debt.

igrot mazon. When a widow and daughters are supported from the estate of the deceased and land of the deceased must be sold for this purpose, the court writes for them in a document which land they may sell for this purpose.
documents of chalitzah. A document given to a woman as proof that she performed chalitzah with her brother-in-law.
and me'unin. A document given to a minor orphan girl as proof that she refused her husband while still a minor.
and these are the documents by which litigants chose their judges. Hilchot Sanhedrin 7:1.
any act of a court. Any action the judges agreed on and wrote in a document.
he returns it. To the one whose name is written in the document, as there is no concern that any problem will result from it.
if he returned it, they are valid and one collects with them. Since not returning is only the initial rule because of a concern, after the fact the document is valid (Maggid Mishneh).
